In the common four-function notation, INTP and ISFP share no combination of function name and attitude. The model describes an emphasis in preference and cannot predict who will stay silent or speak first.

compare_blocks.title: The key difference

compare_blocks.body:
The premise for the table is aligned conditions: the same material, the same chance to speak, the same preparation time. If one is presenting and the other is only observing, the difference in roles may explain what you see. The topic rewrites it too: on a subject both care about, both are talkative; on an irrelevant one, both are silent.

compare_blocks.title: One-minute comparison

compare_blocks.body:
In an unfamiliar room neither may volunteer to lead, and on a familiar topic either may speak first. Quietness depends more on the role, the degree of familiarity and the risk of conflict than on shared letters.

The shared I and P account for part of the resemblance: I turns attention and energy more toward the inner world, such as your own ideas and sorting things out; P describes a preference for keeping options open and continuing to take in information. Other people often misread their not speaking up as having no opinion, when the internal activity is dense; equally, both can settle a question early when the responsibility is clear.

The difference sits on two axes. S/N concerns the information people give more weight: observable facts and experience, or patterns and possibilities. The other is the basis for judgement: whether one standard can be applied consistently, or what the matter means for the people involved. Both axes are available to anyone; the difference is which one you rely on more often.

### The same proposal, two kinds of evidence

In a fictional review, two colleagues have the same proposal, evidence and authority. One line of enquiry is how the proposal defines “improve the experience” and whether it applies that standard consistently. Another is what the proposal would ask of the people delivering it and whose needs it overlooks. Both can also check which figures are measurements and which are estimates.

Both lines of enquiry can improve the same proposal. They illustrate different criteria for a decision. Either colleague can use both, in either order.

That difference is useful in a review meeting. Hearing "there is a problem with this logic" and "this arrangement is wrong for the people involved", do not rush to decide who is more professional — the first offers a gap that can be discussed, the second offers an effect not yet written into the proposal. Ask for a specific case and check what the proposal would require in that situation.

### Why no function is shared between them

This pair differs on S/N and T/F at once, so both perceiving positions and both judging positions change family. In the common four-function notation used here, INTP is Ti–Ne–Si–Fe and ISFP is Fi–Se–Ni–Te: position for position that is Ti against Fi, Ne against Se, Si against Ni, Fe against Te, with no function kept under the same name.

What survives is the inward or outward attitude of each position: both have an inward dominant, an outward auxiliary, an inward third and an outward inferior. No function shares both name and attitude, and the attitude arrangement is identical under this convention. What differs is which set gets used more: logic and possibility, or values and present experience.

Whether the third function is labelled inward or outward is not consistent across published tables. This page uses the common version; the disagreement does not change the first two positions and does not explain how early someone speaks up. Both base descriptions are in the [INTP profile](/en/personality/intp) and the [ISFP profile](/en/personality/isfp).
compare_blocks.title: Why they are easily confused

compare_blocks.body:
The two fictional scenes below are for practising the distinction between the information someone trusts and the reason they decide. Whether training works has to be judged from participant feedback and later use, not from type.

### Choosing examples for a training course

(Fictional scene.) A course for frontline supervisors is about giving feedback. One presenter chooses a counter-intuitive case: a supervisor used the standard feedback form but bundled three unrelated issues into one discussion. The employee stopped offering suggestions for three months. Ask learners what the example shows about how the feedback was delivered, and what they would need to know before they could say why the employee stopped speaking up. The other chooses an everyday scene: a shift leader stops someone at the locker-room door, says two sentences, and that person's whole day changes; the point is to let participants see what tone and setting do.

The two choices serve different learning goals: the first wants participants to see under what conditions a principle fails, the second wants them to recognise a moment they have lived through. Either can work and either can fail — the counter-intuitive case may be dismissed as a one-off incident, and the everyday scene may be remembered as a picture with no method attached.

The check that follows is exploratory, not proof of effect: prepare two questions, one asking "what happened in this example" to see whether participants retained the principle or the picture, and one set in a situation that has not appeared, to see whether they can apply the principle. A trial run with five people in each group can suggest which example better supports each goal; the sample is far too small to prove teaching effect, let alone validate a type difference. For transfer to work, review the actual feedback behaviour afterwards, such as whether later conversations stayed on one issue.

The two ways of choosing are teaching trade-offs, not strategies owned by a type; where both the principle and the situation matter, they can be combined rather than ranked.

### When a friend complains about repeated cancellations

(Fictional scene.) A friend says: "They have changed the time twice now, and I don't know whether I should still go." One response asks first whether the changes were agreed by everyone and what would count as a fair arrangement next time; the other asks first what each change cost the friend, and confirms which commitments in this relationship matter particularly to them.

Both responses can help the friend decide how to arrange the next meeting. Rules alone may miss that the friend has already swapped two shifts for this; feelings alone may miss the practical difficulties other people are facing. One person can raise both kinds of evidence, and the order in which they are raised cannot determine a type.

It helps to ask first: "Do you want someone to listen, or do you want to work out a plan together?" If a plan is wanted, agree on a latest confirmation time next round and state clearly who has to notify the others.

Being easy-going is not the same as having no position. sections.body_md:
In an unfamiliar room neither may volunteer to lead, and on a familiar topic either may speak first. Quietness depends more on the role, the degree of familiarity and the risk of conflict than on shared letters.

The shared I and P account for part of the resemblance: I turns attention and energy more toward the inner world, such as your own ideas and sorting things out; P describes a preference for keeping options open and continuing to take in information. Other people often misread their not speaking up as having no opinion, when the internal activity is dense; equally, both can settle a question early when the responsibility is clear.

The difference sits on two axes. S/N concerns the information people give more weight: observable facts and experience, or patterns and possibilities. The other is the basis for judgement: whether one standard can be applied consistently, or what the matter means for the people involved. Both axes are available to anyone; the difference is which one you rely on more often.

### The same proposal, two kinds of evidence

In a fictional review, two colleagues have the same proposal, evidence and authority. One line of enquiry is how the proposal defines “improve the experience” and whether it applies that standard consistently. Another is what the proposal would ask of the people delivering it and whose needs it overlooks. Both can also check which figures are measurements and which are estimates.

Both lines of enquiry can improve the same proposal. They illustrate different criteria for a decision. Either colleague can use both, in either order.

That difference is useful in a review meeting. Hearing "there is a problem with this logic" and "this arrangement is wrong for the people involved", do not rush to decide who is more professional — the first offers a gap that can be discussed, the second offers an effect not yet written into the proposal. Ask for a specific case and check what the proposal would require in that situation.

### Why no function is shared between them

This pair differs on S/N and T/F at once, so both perceiving positions and both judging positions change family. In the common four-function notation used here, INTP is Ti–Ne–Si–Fe and ISFP is Fi–Se–Ni–Te: position for position that is Ti against Fi, Ne against Se, Si against Ni, Fe against Te, with no function kept under the same name.

What survives is the inward or outward attitude of each position: both have an inward dominant, an outward auxiliary, an inward third and an outward inferior. No function shares both name and attitude, and the attitude arrangement is identical under this convention. What differs is which set gets used more: logic and possibility, or values and present experience.

Whether the third function is labelled inward or outward is not consistent across published tables. This page uses the common version; the disagreement does not change the first two positions and does not explain how early someone speaks up. Both base descriptions are in the [INTP profile](/en/personality/intp) and the [ISFP profile](/en/personality/isfp).

sections.body_md:
The two fictional scenes below are for practising the distinction between the information someone trusts and the reason they decide. Whether training works has to be judged from participant feedback and later use, not from type.

### Choosing examples for a training course

(Fictional scene.) A course for frontline supervisors is about giving feedback. One presenter chooses a counter-intuitive case: a supervisor used the standard feedback form but bundled three unrelated issues into one discussion. The employee stopped offering suggestions for three months. Ask learners what the example shows about how the feedback was delivered, and what they would need to know before they could say why the employee stopped speaking up. The other chooses an everyday scene: a shift leader stops someone at the locker-room door, says two sentences, and that person's whole day changes; the point is to let participants see what tone and setting do.

The two choices serve different learning goals: the first wants participants to see under what conditions a principle fails, the second wants them to recognise a moment they have lived through. Either can work and either can fail — the counter-intuitive case may be dismissed as a one-off incident, and the everyday scene may be remembered as a picture with no method attached.

The check that follows is exploratory, not proof of effect: prepare two questions, one asking "what happened in this example" to see whether participants retained the principle or the picture, and one set in a situation that has not appeared, to see whether they can apply the principle. A trial run with five people in each group can suggest which example better supports each goal; the sample is far too small to prove teaching effect, let alone validate a type difference. For transfer to work, review the actual feedback behaviour afterwards, such as whether later conversations stayed on one issue.

The two ways of choosing are teaching trade-offs, not strategies owned by a type; where both the principle and the situation matter, they can be combined rather than ranked.

### When a friend complains about repeated cancellations

(Fictional scene.) A friend says: "They have changed the time twice now, and I don't know whether I should still go." One response asks first whether the changes were agreed by everyone and what would count as a fair arrangement next time; the other asks first what each change cost the friend, and confirms which commitments in this relationship matter particularly to them.

Both responses can help the friend decide how to arrange the next meeting. Rules alone may miss that the friend has already swapped two shifts for this; feelings alone may miss the practical difficulties other people are facing. One person can raise both kinds of evidence, and the order in which they are raised cannot determine a type.

It helps to ask first: "Do you want someone to listen, or do you want to work out a plan together?" If a plan is wanted, agree on a latest confirmation time next round and state clearly who has to notify the others.
